question:
Patient note:
A 47-year-old man with a decade-long history of alcohol-related chronic liver injury—biopsy three years ago showed stage-3 fibrosis with mild portal tract inflammation and his last hepatology follow-up six months back documented mild thrombocytopenia without encephalopathy—presented to the emergency department after noticing three consecutive jet-black, shiny bowel movements that glued to the toilet porcelain over the preceding twelve hours, accompanied by foul, tar-like odor and a dull epigastric squeeze that intensified whenever he tried to lie flat. He denied dizzy spells, blackout, chest pressure, palpitations, cough, or lower-extremity swelling, and stated that he walked into the hospital unaided but felt “weak and soaked in sweat” while waiting at triage. His regular medications are limited to 40 mg oral furosemide each morning, lactulose as needed for constipation, and an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor he takes sporadically when heartburn flares; he has never been prescribed beta-blockers, anticoagulants, dual antiplatelet therapy, or corticosteroids, and he last ingested non-steroidal anti-inflammatory pills “a couple of months” ago for a dental extraction. Alcohol intake averages four shots of whiskey nightly, though he says he abstained for the last two days because of nausea; he denies intravenous drug use since college, has smoked one pack per day for twenty years, and uses no illicit substances currently. Family history is notable only for a mother with type 2 diabetes; no relatives have bleeding disorders or congestive cardiomyopathy. Review of systems revealed early satiety, occasional right upper-quadrant fullness, easy bruising on the shins, and stable body weight; there were no orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or exertional limitations beyond his usual baseline. On arrival—prior to intravenous access, fluid bolus, antiemetic, vasoactive infusion, blood product administration, or acid suppression—he sat forward on the stretcher, pale, with beads of sweat on the forehead but fully oriented and answering in complete sentences. Manual vital signs obtained by nursing staff showed a narrow pulse pressure with a systolic blood pressure of 90 mm Hg and diastolic of 56 mm Hg, a brisk tachycardia clocked at 128 beats per minute that was regular on the monitor, respiratory rate 24 per minute, oral temperature 37.1 °C, and oxygen saturation 96 % while breathing ambient air. Conjunctival pallor was evident; sclerae were anicteric; oral mucosa appeared tacky with a trace of dried coffee-ground material at the uvula. Spider angiomas peppered the upper chest and there was faint palmar erythema; no digital clubbing or leukonychia was seen. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated at 30°, and there was no peripheral edema. Cardiac auscultation identified a rapid but otherwise unremarkable S1 and S2 without gallops or murmurs. Lungs were clear to auscultation throughout. The abdomen was scaphoid, soft, and mildly tender in the epigastrium on deep palpation, with a firm, 15 cm liver edge palpable two fingerbreadths below the costal margin and a splenic tip just felt on inspiration; percussion suggested a shifting dullness of less than 2 cm and no obvious fluid wave. Bowel sounds were hyperactive. Digital rectal examination produced a smear of black, tarry stool that turned the bedside guaiac card an immediate dark blue. Two 18-gauge antecubital intravenous lines were placed solely for sampling at this juncture, and a type-and-screen was sent but no therapies had yet commenced when initial labs resulted: hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, hematocrit 27 %, mean corpuscular volume 90 fL, platelet count 109 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 7.6 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 52 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL, albumin 2.9 g/dL, international normalized ratio 1.4, sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, and glucose 98 mg/dL. A portable single-view chest radiograph performed concurrently showed clear lung fields and a normal cardiac silhouette; an abdominal upright film revealed a nonspecific gas pattern without free intraperitoneal air. Twelve-lead electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia at 130 bpm with normal intervals and no ischemic ST-T changes. At this point he had received no crystalloid resuscitation, proton pump inhibitor infusion, vasoactive medications, octreotide, or transfusion; he was placed on continuous cardiac and pulse-oximetry monitoring, kept nil per os, an emergent gastroenterology consult was initiated for possible endoscopic hemostasis of presumed upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of chronic hepatic injury, and cross-matched packed red blood cells were requested while serial hematologic indices and vital signs were arranged for close surveillance.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses admission BUN, sex-specific hemoglobin, systolic pressure, pulse, melena, syncope, hepatic disease, and heart failure.
- BUN 52 mg/dL (approximately 18.6 mmol/L urea, in the 10 to <25 mmol/L band): 4 points.
- Hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL in a man (<10): 6 points.
- Systolic BP 90 mmHg (90–99, not <90): 2 points.
- Pulse 128/min (≥100): 1 point.
- Melena confirmed by black, tarry stool: 1 point.
- No syncope: 0 points.
- Documented chronic alcohol-related hepatic disease: 2 points.
- No heart failure: 0 points.
Total: 4 + 6 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 16.
Final answer: 16
